ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Parent-child participants completed a perceptual judgment task on separate tablet computers (Fig. 2: 685 children and 669 parents; Methods). on separate tablet computers.

> Participants were recruited at NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, and invited to complete a brief experiment.

> All participants were fluent in Dutch or English.

> Participants were instructed not to communicate with each other during the session.

> Participants completed the task privately on their own tablet.

> Participants had to move the slider before they could continue.

> Participants were instructed to estimate as accurately as possible.

> In wave 2, participants completed five additional trials in which the source of the social information was not identified as a child or adult.

> Estimates from a linear mixed-effects model predicting social information use (s) from whether participants had selected the observed source, receiver, age, and transmission pathway, with participant as a random intercept, pooling data from Experiments 1 and 2.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the University of Amsterdam (2021-DP-13852).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > .072", Text = "E1 Same, extended to age and parents Waves 1-6 s ~ age_c × transmission × age_group + (1 ｜ppt) 1,183 participants, 5,039 trials Age × horizontal b = 0.019, p = .030 Main text; Fig 2; Table S4 E1 Source choice as a function of age Waves 7-10 Multinomial logistic, transmission ~ age, fitted separately for children and parents Children 834 (4,169 trials); parents 829 (4,145 trials) Vertical preferred in both groups (children, oblique vs. vertical OR = 0.25; parents OR = 0.11); no significant age effects (all p > .072)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 66 columns across 1 data file.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Parent-child participants completed a perceptual judgment task on separate tablet computers (Fig. 2: 685 children and 669 parents; Methods). on separate tablet computers.
Participants were recruited at NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, and invited to complete a brief experiment.
All participants were fluent in Dutch or English.
Participants were instructed not to communicate with each other during the session.
Participants completed the task privately on their own tablet.
Participants had to move the slider before they could continue.
Participants were instructed to estimate as accurately as possible.
In wave 2, participants completed five additional trials in which the source of the social information was not identified as a child or adult.

Estimates from a linear mixed-effects model predicting social information use (s) from whether participants had selected the observed source, receiver, age, and transmission pathway, with participant as a random intercept, pooling data from Experiments 1 and 2.

#### File paths
**20 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 02_P1-E1_all_wave_resemblance.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 06_P2_adult_vs_peer.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 07_P3_children_vs_caregivers.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 08_P4_child_age.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 09_P5_transmission_pathways.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 10_P5-E1_age_transmission_receiver.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 11_E1_source_selection.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 11a_E1_source_selection_plots.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 12_E2_child_chosen_information.R); `_setup.R` to `src/r/_setup.R` (in 13_E3_caregiver_chosen_information.R), and 10 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **5 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 28 scripts: 21 ran without error, 7 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **21 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `06_P2_adult_vs_peer.R` (_setup.R); `07_P3_children_vs_caregivers.R` (_setup.R); `08_P4_child_age.R` (_setup.R); `09_P5_transmission_pathways.R` (_setup.R); `10_P5-E1_age_transmission_receiver.R` (_setup.R); `11_E1_source_selection.R` (_setup.R); `11a_E1_source_selection_plots.R` (_setup.R); `12_E2_child_chosen_information.R` (_setup.R); `13_E3_caregiver_chosen_information.R` (_setup.R); `14_E4_estimation_accuracy.R` (_setup.R); `15_E5_accuracy_by_pathway.R` (_setup.R); `16_E6_self_rated_performance_information.R` (_setup.R); `17_E7_self_rated_performance_accuracy.R` (_setup.R); `17a_SI_S7_active_source_selection.R` (_setup.R); `18_SI_S10_seating_configuration.R` (_setup.R); `19_SI_S11_configuration_choice.R` (_setup.R); `20_SI_distance_discounting.R` (_setup.R); `21_SI_FigureS4_children_waves_7-8.R` (_setup.R); `22_SI_FigureS4_children_waves_9-10.R` (_setup.R); `23_SI_FigureS4_source_choice.R` (_setup.R); `24_SI_assemble_figure_panels.R` (_setup.R). Then these ran to the end: `06_P2_adult_vs_peer.R`, `07_P3_children_vs_caregivers.R`, `08_P4_child_age.R`, `09_P5_transmission_pathways.R`, `10_P5-E1_age_transmission_receiver.R`, `11_E1_source_selection.R`, `11a_E1_source_selection_plots.R`, `12_E2_child_chosen_information.R`, `13_E3_caregiver_chosen_information.R`, `14_E4_estimation_accuracy.R`, `15_E5_accuracy_by_pathway.R`, `16_E6_self_rated_performance_information.R`, `17_E7_self_rated_performance_accuracy.R`, `17a_SI_S7_active_source_selection.R`, `18_SI_S10_seating_configuration.R`, `19_SI_S11_configuration_choice.R`, `20_SI_distance_discounting.R`, `21_SI_FigureS4_children_waves_7-8.R`, `22_SI_FigureS4_children_waves_9-10.R`, `23_SI_FigureS4_source_choice.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **2 scripts looked for 2 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `src/r/_setup.R` to `src/r/src/r/_setup.R` for `02_P1-E1_all_wave_resemblance.R`; `data/nemo_analysis_data.csv` to `src/r/data/nemo_analysis_data.csv` for `23_SI_FigureS4_source_choice.R`. text.text: Human culture depends on people learning from one another.

Cultural evolutionary theory distinguishes three transmission pathways: learning from parents (vertical), non-parental adults (oblique), and peers (horizontal), which differ in how rapidly information spreads within and across generations.

During middle childhood, children's social worlds expand beyond the family, creating opportunities for all three pathways to operate simultaneously, yet their relative strength has rarely been compared directly.
Using 1,262 dyads of 6-13 year-olds and their parents, we examined the relative strength of vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission in two complementary behavioral experiments.
Participants either received information from, or chose between, their own parent or child, an unrelated adult or child, and a peer while completing an estimation task.
This design allowed us to separate two components of cultural transmission: whom people choose to learn from and how strongly they use information once it has been acquired.
Vertical transmission emerged as the strongest pathway.

This advantage was driven primarily by source selection, as children and parents overwhelmingly selected one another as information sources, with parents learning from their own child providing evidence for reverse vertical transmission.
Once information had been acquired, however, information weighting differed little between vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission.
Instead, developmental differences dominated: social information use declined markedly across middle childhood and remained consistently higher in children than in parents.
Together, these findings suggest that the relative strength of cultural transmission pathways is determined primarily by source selection rather than information weighting.
Humans acquire much of what they know from other people (1) (2) (3).
text.formatted: Humans acquire much of what they know from other people <ref type="bibr">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Parents pass on knowledge and skills to their children, children learn from teachers and other adults, and peers learn from one another.
Through such social learning, knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors that make up human culture spread between individuals and across generations (4) (5) (6) (7) (8).
text.formatted: Through such social learning, knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors that make up human culture spread between individuals and across generations <ref type="bibr">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Which sources people learn from therefore shapes both what individuals come to know and how information moves through populations.

Information transmitted primarily from parents to children can spread only as new generations acquire it, whereas information acquired from peers or unrelated adults can diffuse more rapidly among individuals within the same generation (4, 5, 9).
text.formatted: Information transmitted primarily from parents to children can spread only as new generations acquire it, whereas information acquired from peers or unrelated adults can diffuse more rapidly among individuals within the same generation <ref type="bibr">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the importance of these different routes for cultural stability and change, little is known about their relative strength when they operate side by side, or about the individual-level processes that make one route more influential than another.

Cultural evolutionary theory formalizes these routes as vertical transmission from parent to offspring, oblique transmission from unrelated adults to younger generations, and horizontal transmission between members of the same generation (4, 5, 7, (10) (11) (12) (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: Cultural evolutionary theory formalizes these routes as vertical transmission from parent to offspring, oblique transmission from unrelated adults to younger generations, and horizontal transmission between members of the same generation <ref type="bibr">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: These transmission pathways provide a powerful abstraction for studying cultural dynamics, but their effective strength emerges from the behavior of individual learners.
A pathway can be influential because people preferentially turn to that source for information, because they place greater weight on its information once acquired, or both.

Moreover, although transmission across generations is typically considered from older to younger individuals, information may also flow in the opposite direction, with children serving as sources for adults (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: Moreover, although transmission across generations is typically considered from older to younger individuals, information may also flow in the opposite direction, with children serving as sources for adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we provide a controlled experimental comparison of vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission and separate these two behavioral components: whom people choose to learn from and how strongly they use the information they acquire.
As children develop, the range of people from whom they can acquire information expands.
Early in childhood, parents are especially available and serve as primary sources of socially transmitted information (19) (20) (21).

text.text: As children's social worlds broaden, interactions with peers and unrelated adults become increasingly common (16, 19, (22) (23) (24) (25) (26) (27).

text.text: During middle childhood (approximately 6-13 years), these expanding social environments create opportunities for vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission to operate alongside one another (17, 19, 24, 28, 29).

text.text: Middle childhood therefore provides a particularly informative period for examining both the pathways through which children acquire information and their role in transmitting it.

Despite extensive interest in social learning, developmental research has primarily examined changes in children's sensitivity to different social learning cues, such as expertise, familiarity, or age (31-33, 35, 37-43).

text.text: Some experiments have directly compared influence from peers and adults, but these examined only a subset of transmission pathways, often in adolescents rather than across middle childhood (31, 44, 45).

text.text: Field studies have taken a broader approach, estimating or reconstructing vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission from reported learning relationships, cultural similarity, or social networks (46) (47) (48) (49).

text.text: However, the relative strength of the three pathways is difficult to infer by comparing across studies because they differ in tasks, populations, and the kinds of information that is transmitted, ranging from social influence on decisions to the transmission of skills, technologies, and factual knowledge (25, 38, (50) (51) (52) (53).

text.text: Direct experimental comparison of all three pathways additionally requires multiple generations to participate within the same controlled setting, which is logistically difficult to organize.
Taken together, these limitations have left the relative strength of the major transmission pathways, and how it changes over development, largely unresolved.

We address these issues by recruiting 1,262 parent-child dyads with children aged 6-13 years in a large science museum, who completed an estimation task in which they could adjust their initial estimates after observing social information (Fig. 1).

text.text: We conducted two experiments that manipulated the source of social information, allowing us to operationalize vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission within a shared behavioral framework and quantify their relative strength directly.
Across experiments, participants either received or selected social information from their parent or child (vertical), an unrelated adult or child (oblique), or a same-generation other (horizontal).

Together, the two experiments characterize social transmission along two complementary dimensions (whom individuals choose to learn from and how strongly they use social information once acquiredhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mVZRQO while allowing us to compare transmission both within and across generations, including from children to parents.  55 )).

text.text: On each trial, participants viewed an image containing 50-100 animals for 6 seconds and entered a first estimate (E₁) by positioning a slider.
They then observed the estimate of another participant (X), displayed together with their own first estimate (E₁) on the slider, before entering a second estimate (E₂).
In Experiment 1, the social information source was assigned; in Experiment 2, participants chose their source.
B. Social information use was quantified as s = (E₂ -E₁) / (X -E₁), capturing the relative extent of moving one's estimate toward the social information on a given trial.
Each participant's mean adjustment across trials is denoted S. C. The three transmission pathways.
In the vertical pathway, children received the estimate of their own parent (SV), while parents received that of their child (SRV, where R in the subscript denotes "reverse").
In the oblique pathway, children received an estimate from an unrelated adult (SO); parents received an estimate from an unrelated child (SRO).
In the horizontal pathway, participants received the estimate from another individual of the same generation (SH).
We formulated predictions about both components of transmission.

First, for how strongly social information is used, we predicted that children would rely more heavily on it than adults, and that this reliance would decline across childhood and adolescence as individuals accumulate their own knowledge and experience.

Given the prominent role of parents as information sources early in development, we further predicted that children would weigh information from parents more strongly than information from unrelated adults or peers, particularly at younger ages.

Second, for whom individuals choose to learn from, we predicted source preferences to shift across middle childhood, from parents toward peers and unrelated adults as children's social environments expand beyond the family.

Finally, our design allowed us to test for intergenerational resemblance in social information use and to look for evidence consistent with reverse transmission, whereby younger generations contribute adaptively relevant information to older generations (16, 36).

Despite the central role of vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission in accounts of cultural change, it has remained unclear how strongly these pathways operate relative to one another when directly compared.

Across two experiments using 1,281 parent-child dyads, we made this comparison while separating two components of social transmission: whom people choose to learn from, and how strongly they use social information once they have it.
These two components behaved differently.
Information weighting was largely indifferent to its source.
Children and parents adjusted their estimates about as much toward a parent, an unrelated adult, or a peer, whether the source was assigned or freely chosen.
By contrast, source selection was not indifferent.
Given a free choice, children and parents overwhelmingly selected each other, on roughly two thirds of trials, and did so across the whole child-age range we studied.
The predominance of vertical transmission in our data therefore arose mainly from source selection rather than information weighting.
We also found evidence for transmission in the opposite generational direction, with adults incorporating information from children.
This distinction between source selection and information weighting adds deeper insights into the behavioral mechanisms underlying transmission pathways studied in cultural evolutionary theory.

Vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission provide a useful abstraction for understanding how information moves through populations (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MVSXMp but the strength of these pathways ultimately emerges from the behavior of individual learners.
text.formatted: Vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission provide a useful abstraction for understanding how information moves through populations (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MVSXMp">4, 5, 10, 12),</ref> but the strength of these pathways ultimately emerges from the behavior of individual learners.

text.text: Our findings show that similar pathway-level patterns can arise from different underlying processes.

In our study, differences between pathways arose almost entirely from source selection: when vertical, oblique, and horizontal sources were equally available, children and parents overwhelmingly selected their own family member, yet once information had been acquired, they weighted it similarly regardless of its source.
Distinguishing these processes can therefore help explain not only which pathways dominate cultural transmission, but why they do so.
What drives the source-selection patterns remains an important question.

In our study, vertical sources were familiar family members whereas alternative sources were generally unfamiliar, so the preference for vertical sources may reflect familiarity or other benefits of consulting a known person as well as the transmission pathway itself.

Moreover, our oblique pathway was deliberately operationalized as an unfamiliar adult or child without any explicit cues to expertise, whereas real-world oblique transmission often involves familiar or knowledgeable individuals such as teachers and experts (4, 30, 59).
text.formatted: Moreover, our oblique pathway was deliberately operationalized as an unfamiliar adult or child without any explicit cues to expertise, whereas real-world oblique transmission often involves familiar or knowledgeable individuals such as teachers and experts <ref type="bibr">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59)</ref>.

text.text: Source preferences may also depend on what is being learned: developmental research shows that children selectively turn to different informants depending on characteristics such as their knowledge or expertise and the learning domain (30) (31) (32) (33).
text.formatted: Source preferences may also depend on what is being learned: developmental research shows that children selectively turn to different informants depending on characteristics such as their knowledge or expertise and the learning domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, in our data, children's strong preference for their parent did not diminish with age, despite peers becoming increasingly prominent in children's social lives.

This apparent contrast may partly reflect source availability: across development, children tend to spend less and less time with family and more time with peers (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ftRDEl increasing opportunities for horizontal transmission.
text.formatted: This apparent contrast may partly reflect source availability: across development, children tend to spend less and less time with family and more time with peers (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ftRDEl">60),</ref> increasing opportunities for horizontal transmission.

text.text: Greater peer influence in everyday life may therefore arise partly from greater opportunities for peer transmission, rather than from an increasing preference for peers when different sources are equally available.
Future work could independently vary familiarity, expertise, and learning domain to establish which characteristics shape source selection.
The second clear pattern in our data was developmental.
Children used more social information than parents at every age and in every transmission pathway.
Parents' reliance was close to the level typically observed in adults, who tend to move only modestly toward social information (35, 55, 61).
text.formatted: Parents' reliance was close to the level typically observed in adults, who tend to move only modestly toward social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">61)</ref>.

text.text: Children's reliance on social information declined steadily across middle childhood, consistent with accounts in which social learning is most valuable early in life, when personal knowledge is limited and uncertainty about one's own judgment is high (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XSiaWk and with previous work documenting a decline in social information use from childhood into adulthood (34, 35, 64).
text.formatted: Children's reliance on social information declined steadily across middle childhood, consistent with accounts in which social learning is most valuable early in life, when personal knowledge is limited and uncertainty about one's own judgment is high (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XSiaWk">4, 36, 58, 62, 63),</ref> and with previous work documenting a decline in social information use from childhood into adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">64)</ref>.

text.text: This decline was somewhat weaker when information came from peers.

Thus, peers did not become more influential in absolute terms, but their influence increased relative to other sources with age, consistent with the growing relative importance of peers over development (65) (66) (67).
text.formatted: Thus, peers did not become more influential in absolute terms, but their influence increased relative to other sources with age, consistent with the growing relative importance of peers over development <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(65)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(66)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(67)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, development primarily changed how strongly children used social information rather than whom they chose to learn from: overall social information use declined across middle childhood, while the relative prominence of vertical transmission remained stable.
Parents' and other adults' behavior points to transmission from younger to older generations, an understudied phenomenon in the field of cultural evolution (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: Parents' and other adults' behavior points to transmission from younger to older generations, an understudied phenomenon in the field of cultural evolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings provide experimental evidence that adults also learn from children, both vertically from their own child and obliquely from unrelated children.
Importantly, participants made their judgments privately, so parents were under no social pressure to adjust their estimates toward those of their child or signal openness to do so.

Rather, they voluntarily incorporated information provided by their own child, suggesting genuine reverse vertical transmission by integrating social information from their child into their judgments rather than public conformity.
This reverse pathway could have consequences for how information spreads through populations.

For example, innovations originating in younger generations may diffuse more rapidly when they are transmitted upward to parents, who can subsequently transmit them to other adults or to the next generation (68) (69) (70).
text.formatted: For example, innovations originating in younger generations may diffuse more rapidly when they are transmitted upward to parents, who can subsequently transmit them to other adults or to the next generation <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(68)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(69)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(70)</ref>.

text.text: Such reverse transmission may be particularly important during periods of rapid social or technological change, when younger generations encounter or adopt novel knowledge and practices before their parents do.

In these circumstances, children can provide a route through which innovations spread from younger to older generations, potentially accelerating their diffusion beyond the cohort in which they first emerge (16, 18, 36, 71).
text.formatted: In these circumstances, children can provide a route through which innovations spread from younger to older generations, potentially accelerating their diffusion beyond the cohort in which they first emerge <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">71)</ref>.

text.text: Our controlled design necessarily held several features of real-world transmission constant, providing directions for future work.

First, the BEAST provides a reliable measure of social information use that correlates with behavior in other social-learning tasks, suggesting that it captures meaningful variation in people's broader propensity to use social information (34, 55).
text.formatted: First, the BEAST provides a reliable measure of social information use that correlates with behavior in other social-learning tasks, suggesting that it captures meaningful variation in people's broader propensity to use social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">55)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the task used here involves estimates with an objectively correct answer.

Whether the same decomposition applies to domains without a single correct answer, such as norms, identity, or values, remains an important question, particularly as peers become increasingly influential during adolescence (27, 34, 47, 72).
text.formatted: Whether the same decomposition applies to domains without a single correct answer, such as norms, identity, or values, remains an important question, particularly as peers become increasingly influential during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">72)</ref>.

text.text: Second, extending the developmental range into adolescence would be particularly informative.

Adolescence brings further changes in social environments and increasing opportunities for learning from peers and non-parental others (16https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UqGkdr 19, (22) (23) (24) (25) (26) 45) , allowing tests of whether the stable source preferences observed across middle childhood persist as peer relationships become more prominent.
text.formatted: Adolescence brings further changes in social environments and increasing opportunities for learning from peers and non-parental others <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UqGkdr">,</ref> allowing tests of whether the stable source preferences observed across middle childhood persist as peer relationships become more prominent.

text.text: Third, our comparison necessarily simplifies the diversity of relationships within each transmission pathway.

Siblings are an especially important omission: depending on their relative ages, they may provide horizontal or age-structured social-learning opportunities and are both familiar and frequently available sources of information.

Including siblings in an experimental design like the one we use here would therefore help establish how kinship, familiarity, age, and transmission pathway jointly shape source selection and information weighting.

Finally, our sample was cross-sectional; longitudinal and network-based studies will be needed to trace how source selection and social information use change within individuals, and how information acquired by children subsequently spreads through families and wider social networks.

By comparing vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission within parent-child dyads, this study suggests that transmission pathways are shaped less by how strongly social information is used than by whom learners choose to turn to.

Across development, children became less receptive to social information, reducing how much was transmitted overall, while a stable preference for family members maintained the prominence of vertical transmission.
Evidence for transmission from children to adults further shows that information can flow across generations in both directions, including within families.

By providing a direct experimental comparison of the relative strength of the three transmission pathways, our findings contribute to a behavioral foundation for cultural evolutionary models, showing that transmission rates emerge from both source selection and information weighting.

Understanding how these two processes vary across individuals, relationships, and environments may therefore be key to explaining how human cultures simultaneously preserve knowledge and remain capable of change.
Participants were recruited at NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, and invited to complete a brief experiment.
All participants were fluent in Dutch or English.
Sessions lasted about 15 minutes and took place in a dedicated testing space in the museum.
Participants were instructed not to communicate with each other during the session.
Data were collected across 10 waves between 2021 and 2025.

The two experiments shared the same core task but differed in whether the information source was assigned (Experiment 1) or chosen (Experiment 2); for additional variations in terms of procedure, see below.
The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the University of Amsterdam (2021-DP-13852).

After excluding sessions involving task-relevant communication, insufficient task comprehension, or participants who were not a parent-child dyad, we excluded participants younger than 6 years (who generally showed poor understanding) or with missing age, as well as those with unusually poor performance (mean absolute error exceeding 3 median absolute deviations from the sample median).
Furthermore, as preregistered, we excluded trials in which participants adjusted away from the social information or beyond the observed estimate (corresponding to s < 0 or s > 1; see Task below).
text.formatted: Furthermore, as preregistered, we excluded trials in which participants adjusted away from the social information or beyond the observed estimate (corresponding to s < 0 or s > 1; see Task below).

text.text: For the parent-child resemblance analysis (Fig. 4A; Fig. S1), we additionally required at least three trials with adjustments within the0 ≤ s ≤ 1 range per participant.

text.text: The final sample consisted of 1,281 parent-child dyads, including 1,262 with children aged 6-13 years and 19 with children aged 14-18 years (children: mean age = 9.0 years, SD = 2.0; parents: mean age = 41.9 years, SD = 5.42).
The 19 dyads with children aged 14-18 years were retained in the statistical analyses to avoid unnecessarily excluding valid observations, but omitted from figures focusing on middle childhood.
Because exclusions were applied to each participant individually, the number of parents and children differs slightly in analyses that do not require both dyad members.
Experiment 1 was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/9xn87).

We report the full correspondence between the preregistered analyses and those presented in this paper, including the preregistered results in their original form, in Table S1.

text.text: Task.
Social information use was measured with the Berlin Estimate Adjustment Task (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Social information use was measured with the Berlin Estimate Adjustment Task (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants completed the task privately on their own tablet.

On each trial, participants viewed an image of a group of animals (between 50 and 100) for 6 seconds and entered an initial estimate of the number of animals shown (E₁) on a slider ranging from 0 to 150, initialized at 0.
Participants had to move the slider before they could continue.
Participants were instructed to estimate as accurately as possible.

After entering their first estimate, they observed social information in the form of another participant's estimate (X), displayed alongside their own first estimate, and entered a second estimate (E₂).
No performance feedback was provided between trials.

Trial-level social information use was quantified as the relative adjustment toward the social information, s = (E₂ -E₁) / (X -E₁), where s = 0 indicates no adjustment and s = 1 indicates adoption of the observed estimate.
Each participant's overall social information use (S) was defined as their mean s across included trials.

The experiment was programmed in the LIONESS Lab (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FC0lXA) and administered on Samsung Galaxy Tab S7 tablets (12.4 inch) running the Fully Kiosk Browser app (version 1.56.2-play).

Design.

The study comprised two experiments contrasting three transmission pathways: vertical (between parent and child), oblique (between a child and an unrelated adult, or a parent and unrelated child), and horizontal (between same-aged peers; Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The study comprised two experiments contrasting three transmission pathways: vertical (between parent and child), oblique (between a child and an unrelated adult, or a parent and unrelated child), and horizontal (between same-aged peers; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The oblique pathway was operationalized without cues to expertise or prestige.
In both experiments, all responses (source choices and estimates) were entered privately on each participant's own tablet, so that a co-present family member could not observe or influence them.
Experiment 1 (preregistered) assigned the source of social information, in a between-subjects design.
Parent-child dyads completed the task independently, although two dyads could be tested simultaneously in the same testing space.
Vertical social information was generated live by the participant's co-present family member, so participants saw an estimate their parent or child had just entered.
Oblique and horizontal social information consisted of estimates from different participants who had completed the task previously.
Child sources were matched to the age of the child in the focal dyad, whereas adult sources were drawn from previous adult participants.

To keep the informational value of social information comparable across sources, prerecorded estimates were selected to fall in the direction of the true value (T), approximately 20% away from the participant's own estimate (55).
text.formatted: To keep the informational value of social information comparable across sources, prerecorded estimates were selected to fall in the direction of the true value (T), approximately 20% away from the participant's own estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(55)</ref>.

text.text: So, target values were set near 1.2 × E₁ when E₁ < T and near 0.8 × E₁ when E₁ > T, with the closest available prerecorded estimate selected subject to the relevant source constraint.
text.formatted: So, target values were set near 1.2 × E₁ when E₁ < T and near 0.8 × E₁ when E₁ > T, with the closest available prerecorded estimate selected subject to the relevant source constraint.

text.text: Oblique and horizontal social information was thus controlled, whereas vertical social information was not.

For children, social information use (s) did not vary systematically with the distance between the first estimate and the social information, whereas parents weighted more distant social information less strongly (Fig. S3).
text.formatted: For children, social information use (s) did not vary systematically with the distance between the first estimate and the social information, whereas parents weighted more distant social information less strongly (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S3</ref>).

text.text: Thus, distancedependent weighting is unlikely to account for our main developmental results.
Experiment 2 allowed participants to choose their source separately on each trial from three options: Parent (vertical), Adult (oblique), or Peer (horizontal).
The experiment was conducted in two slightly different setups.
In waves 7-8, parent-child dyads formed separate experimental units.

Vertical social information was generated live by the co-present family member, whereas oblique and horizontal information came from prerecorded estimates of previous participants, calibrated as in Experiment 1.

In waves 9-10, two parent-child dyads participated simultaneously, forming a single experimental unit and allowing information from all three source types to be generated live by co-present participants.
Results were similar across these setups, supporting their inclusion in the same analyses.

Information weighting showed little evidence of differences (Table S10), while the physical presence of another family was associated with a slight increase in their selection, mostly in oblique transmission (children +5.1 percentage points (pp), adults +6.0 pp; Fig. S4, Table S11).

These "source-neutral" trials closely followed the original BEAST procedure (55) and were included to test parent-child resemblance in social information use independently of source identity.

text.text: Procedure.
Participants entered their age and gender on the tablet before beginning the task, then completed the task seated near their parent or child.
Seating arrangements varied somewhat across data collection waves because of changes in museum facilities (e.g., face-toface, facing away, or separated by a divider).

Because all responses were entered privately on individual tablets, participants could not observe one another's decisions, and analyses indicated no meaningful effect of seating arrangement on social information use (Table S10).

Translations below are based on their Dutch originals.
At the start of each session, the experimenter communicated the following points in the order shown.
The wording did not need to be verbatim: experimenters presented the instructions naturally and in language appropriate for children aged six years and older.
At least one parent of each participating child was present during the instructions.
Welcome and general introduction.
"Welcome!
You are going to take part in an experiment about decision-making from the Department of Psychology at the University of Amsterdam.
We cannot tell you exactly what the experiment is about beforehand, but we will explain this afterwards."
Information and voluntary participation.
"Before we start, you will receive this information letter.
The most important things to know are that your data will be anonymous (we cannot tell who you are from your data) and that you can stop participating at any time."
→ Hand out the tablets.
"There is a short task on the tablet, and you will also see instructions on the screen.
You will see pictures with animals and your task is to estimate as accurately as possible how many animals there are, using a slider.
After making your first estimate, you will see another person's estimate.
You can then make a second estimate.
The other person saw the same picture and was also asked to estimate the number of animals as accurately as possible."
In waves 1-8, when estimates from previous participants could be shown, we added: "Some of these estimates come from people who previously visited the museum and completed this task.
We stored their answers so that we can show them to you."
"In each round, you can choose whose estimate you want to see: your own parent [for parents: your own child], another adult, or another child."
In waves 7-8 we added: "The other adult and child completed the task previously."
In waves 9-10 we added "the other adult and child are the members of the other family participating now with you in the same session".
This screenshot shows the instructions for Experiment 2, in which participants chose whose estimate they wanted to see.
The three other players had been explicitly introduced during the oral instructions (see above): for children, their own parent, another adult, and another child.
For parents, "your parent" was replaced by "your child."
In Experiment 1, the source was assigned.

The screen specified that participants would see the estimate of their own parent/child in the vertical condition, or of another adult/child who had completed the task previously in the oblique/horizontal conditions, consistent with the preceding oral instructions.
The screen read: "After entering your estimate, you will see the estimate of [source].
text.formatted: The screen read: "After entering your estimate, you will see the estimate of <ref type="bibr">[source]</ref>.

text.text: Then you can make a second estimate of how many animals there were.
There are five rounds in total."
In the oblique and horizontal conditions, this was followed by: "This task has been completed by many museum visitors.
In each round you will see the estimate of a different person."
After this screen, the task started.
At the start of each round, the participants observed an image with a group of animals.
This screenshot shows the stimulus presented in the first round.
The five rounds always presented the same stimuli in a fixed order: 93 ladybugs, 78 dragonflies, 59 butterflies, 74 bees, and 69 stag beetles.
The slider was initialized at 0, and participants could not continue without moving it.
The number displayed above the slider updated as the slider was moved.
This screen was shown only in Experiment 2, in which participants selected the source.
In Experiment 1, the source was assigned.
For parents, the top left screen shows a smaller icon with "My child" (see next screenshot).
For parents, "My parent" was replaced by "My child"; all other source options were unchanged.
Like the previous screen, this screen was only shown in Experiment 2.
Participants then entered a second estimate using the same slider.
The social information (the other person's estimate) was shown in red above the slider.
At the end of the task, participants received feedback on the accuracy of their first and second estimates and their social information use.
This feedback was provided to encourage discussion between children and their parents about social influence, as required by the museum.

text.text: After each round, the task returned to the stimulus screen shown above and the same sequence was repeated with the next animal species, for five rounds in total.
This ladder was used to measure self-rated performance.
Fig 1.
Experimental setup and transmission pathways.
A. Trial structure of the Berlin Estimate Adjustment Task (BEAST (55)).
On each trial, participants viewed an image containing 50-100 animals for 6 seconds and entered a first estimate (E₁) by positioning a slider.
They then observed the estimate of another participant (X), displayed together with their own first estimate (E₁) on the slider, before entering a second estimate (E₂).
In Experiment 1, the social information source was assigned; in Experiment 2, participants chose their source.
B. Social information use was quantified as s = (E₂ -E₁) / (X -E₁), capturing the relative extent of moving one's estimate toward the social information on a given trial.
Each participant's mean adjustment across trials is denoted S. C. The three transmission pathways.
In the vertical pathway, children received the estimate of their own parent (SV), while parents received that of their child (SRV, where R in the subscript denotes "reverse").
In the oblique pathway, children received an estimate from an unrelated adult (SO); parents received an estimate from an unrelated child (SRO).
In the horizontal pathway, participants received the estimate from another individual of the same generation (SH).
Fig 3.
Source selection and information use across development (Experiment 2).
A-B, Proportion of trials in which participants selected vertical (red), oblique (green), or horizontal (blue) sources, plotted against child age.
A, children; B, parents.
Sample sizes (distinct participants) are shown above each bar.
C-D, Mean social information use (S) following source selection, plotted against child age.
Symbols represent per-age means, with symbol size proportional to sample size.
Lines show linear mixed-effects model predictions with 95% confidence intervals.
The x-axis corresponds to the age of the child in each dyad; parent data are plotted at their child's age.
The dotted blue line in D indicates adults' mean social information use when receiving information from another adult (horizontal transmission), for which childage is not applicable.
Fig 4.
Parent-child resemblance, estimation accuracy, and self-rated performance.

A. Children's social information use (Schild) plotted against their parents' social information use (Sparent) across 1,281 parent-child dyads, where S denotes each participant's mean adjustment toward social information across trials (Fig 1).
Each point represents one dyad; the line shows the fitted linear regression with 95% confidence intervals.

B-C, Mean proportional estimation error (lower values indicate greater accuracy) before (E₁, dashed) and after (E₂, solid) incorporating social information, plotted against age for children (B) and parents (C).
Shaded bands show 95% confidence intervals around LOESS smoothers.
D. Mean proportional estimation error before and after social information by transmission pathway, shown separately for children (red) and parents (blue).
Numerical labels indicate mean estimation error (see Fig S2 for breakdown by experiment).
E-F, Associations between self-rated performance and social information use (E) and first-estimate accuracy (F) for children (red) and parents (blue).
Lines show fitted regressions with 95% confidence intervals.
Fig S2.
Estimation accuracy before and after social information by transmission pathway and experiment.
Mean proportional estimation error is shown for children (A, red) and parents (B, blue).
Gray points indicate error before social information; colored open circles indicate error after social information.
Numerical labels give the corresponding means; lower values indicate greater accuracy.
V denotes vertical transmission pooled across Experiments 1 and 2.
O1 and O2 denote oblique transmission in Experiments 1 and 2, respectively; H1 and H2 denote horizontal transmission in Experiments 1 and 2, respectively.
